human_tolerance.notes: Wikipedia places the species in urban parks as well as deciduous woodland, and it habitually raids bird feeders and garden beds; it is bold but flees to cover quickly. human_tolerance thresholds are authored judgement for suburban-lot placement.

phases.name: dormancy
phases.note: Long periods of hibernation through the winter; the source says the chipmunk 'may enter long periods of hibernation', so the phase length is authored.

phases.name: mating
phases.note: First breeding season, February to April; the only period the solitary adults interact, apart from mothers and pups.

phases.name: young
phases.note: Females usually produce one or two litters of three to five young, with the second breeding season from June to August; pups stay with their mothers for about six to eight weeks.

phases.name: caching
phases.note: Food is carried in cheek pouches and stored for the winter; autumn is when the burrow stores are filled.

phases.name: moult
phases.note: Molt occurs once or twice a year, during May or June and sometimes again in October; the second window is folded into the caching phase here.

vocalizations.description: A sharp repeated chip, one of the five stereotyped sounds in the species' repertoire, given at a perceived threat or a rival; usually accompanied by a darting run for cover.
A lower, fuller chuck used at closer range or when the animal is startled, the counterpart to the chip in the documented five-sound repertoire.
Rapid chattering directed at an intruder at the burrow, from an animal defending its own entrance.
A trilling call measured at about 130 trills per minute, used between individuals of the documented five-sound repertoire.
The whistle or squeal of the documented repertoire, a high thin note given at close approach or when an animal is handled.

external.note: GBIF usage key 2437438 and Wikidata Q692664 confirmed from the live APIs; iNaturalist taxon id 46217 from the iNaturalist taxa API. No ITIS TSN or NCBI taxon id is recorded because neither was confirmed from a query during this contribution; those keys are optional.

common_names.note: English name from GBIF and Wikipedia. The French, German and Dutch labels are the standard names for the species in those languages from Wikipedia sitelinks; they are not independently sourced here.

conservation.note: Least Concern, carried on Wikidata. The IUCN page itself was not used, because it is not openly licensed, so this rests on the Wikidata statement alone rather than on a second independent source.

range.note: Country list from Wikipedia: eastern North America, in deciduous wooded areas and urban parks throughout the eastern United States and southern Canada, so the United States and Canada are recorded and no other country is claimed. Köppen classes are coarse authored judgement from that range and include Dfa and Dfb for the Ontario target region.

traits.limb_count.note: Wikipedia describes four toes on each front leg and five on each hind leg.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: Wikipedia says the eastern chipmunk can climb trees well and spends most of its day foraging on the ground, so walk, hop and climb are modeled.

traits.nest_type.note: Constructs underground nests with extensive tunnel systems and several entrances, lined with leaves, rocks and sticks.

traits.perching.note: It climbs trees well rather than perching habitually, so perching is false.

traits.length_m.note: Wikipedia gives about 30 cm including the tail. That is a rounded 'about' value, not a precise measurement range, so 0.30 m carries no more precision than the source.

traits.lifespan_y.note: Wikipedia states that on average eastern chipmunks live three or more years in the wild, and up to eight in captivity; the wild figure is recorded.

traits.home_range_ha.note: Judgement: the source says the animal defends its own burrow and lives a solitary life but gives no range area, so 0.4 ha is an authored figure for a small territorial ground forager.

traits.diet.note: Wikipedia lists bulbs, seeds, fruits, nuts, green plants, mushrooms, insects, worms and bird eggs. The shares are authored from that list, mapping nuts to mast, green plants and bulbs to browse, and insects and worms to invertebrate; no single item is quantified in the source, so the split is judgement.

traits.social.note: Wikipedia says the species defends its burrow and lives a solitary life except during mating season and while pups are with their mothers.

traits.activity_pattern.note: Wikipedia says the chipmunk is mainly active during the day, spending most of its day foraging.

traits.defense.note: The documented chip, chuck, chatter and whistle calls and the strong preference for cover near the burrow indicate escape rather than standing ground; modeled as Flee.

traits.wariness.note: Judgement: bold around people and feeders, but relies heavily on cover and flees quickly, so wariness is set moderate.

habitat.use.note: Wikipedia describes deciduous wooded areas and urban parks, with the animal climbing trees well but foraging mostly on the ground; the shares are authored.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: The underground burrow with several entrances is the shelter that matters most, and is recorded here with the cavity tag the schema offers for enclosed dens, since the schema has no separate burrow tag for habitat.shelter_tag. traits.nest_type carries the more accurate 'Burrow'.

habitat.resources.note: Food tags follow the sourced diet; cavity, shrub_thicket and perch follow the documented preference for rocky areas, brush or log piles and shrubs for cover, and for tree climbing.

habitat.requires.note: Judgement for the behavior program: an animal that lives in a defended burrow needs at least one nearby cavity in the simulation.

habitat.suitability.note: Judgement from the habitat description - deciduous woodland edge and urban parks with cover nearby - with curves authored for suburban-lot placement.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: Wikipedia places the species in urban parks; feeder and garden-raid boldness is implied rather than stated. The numeric thresholds are authored judgement for simulation placement.

seasonal.strategy.note: Wikipedia says that during winter the chipmunk may enter long periods of hibernation, so Hibernation is used, with 'may' reflected in the dormancy phase being a long authored window rather than a fixed behaviour.

seasonal.triggers.note: Judgement. The schema requires seasonal.triggers for a Hibernation strategy and the source article gives no temperature threshold, only that the chipmunk may enter long periods of hibernation in winter. 4 C sustained for five days is an authored figure in the range of a rodent that shelters in a burrow with a stable temperature; it is not a quoted value.

seasonal.phases.note: Winter hibernation, February to April and June to August breeding seasons, one or two litters of three to five young, six to eight weeks with the mother, and molt in May or June (sometimes October) all come from Wikipedia. Month-day boundaries and the moult window are authored.

seasonal.life_stages.note: The juvenile stage follows the sourced six to eight weeks with the mother; duration and scale are simulation judgement.

behavior.note: Authored parameters for fsm-ground-forager-v1: daytime ground foraging on seed, a short flee distance for a fast-moving rodent, and a rest window set for a diurnal species.

vocalizations.chip.note: Wikipedia names the chip as one of five stereotyped sounds in the repertoire.

vocalizations.chuck.note: Wikipedia names the chuck as one of the five stereotyped sounds.

vocalizations.chatter.note: Wikipedia names chatter as one of the five sounds and describes burrow defence; the intruder-directed context and cooldown are authored.

vocalizations.trill.note: Wikipedia names the trills and measures them at about 130 trills per minute.

vocalizations.whistle.note: Wikipedia names the whistle or squeal in the repertoire; the close-approach context and cooldown are authored.

look.note: Wikipedia describes reddish-brown fur on the upper body, five dark brown stripes contrasting with light brown stripes along the back, a dark tail, lighter fur below, a tawny stripe running from the whiskers to below the ears and light stripes over the eyes. Palette and block proportions are authored judgement for a stylised model.
